title: The market inspector weighs a baker's bread
hook: A 1657 drawing from Istanbul: the muhtasib checks that a loaf really weighs what the baker charges for.
summary: The muhtasib walked the market with scales. Bakers, butchers and grocers could be fined or shamed in public for short weights, watered milk or false prices. This drawing comes from the costume book a Swedish envoy had made in Istanbul. Why this matters: Before consumer law, this was the person who stood between an ordinary shopper and a dishonest scale.
why: Before consumer law, this was the person who stood between an ordinary shopper and a dishonest scale.
creator: Rålamb Costume Book

title: A glass weight that kept money honest
hook: Stamped glass disc from Egypt, made around 808–810, used to check that a gold coin was full weight.
summary: Coins were often clipped or worn down. Officials issued glass weights stamped with a name, and a merchant could set a coin on one pan of a balance and this weight on the other. Glass was used because it cannot be shaved without leaving a mark. Why this matters: A cheap, tamper-proof tool meant a stranger's coin could be trusted, which is how long-distance trade worked.
why: A cheap, tamper-proof tool meant a stranger's coin could be trusted, which is how long-distance trade worked.
rights_status: open licence: Public domain (Met Open Access)

title: Another glass check-weight from Egypt
hook: Stamped glass weights like this were the market's shared measure.
summary: Many glass weights survive from medieval Egypt, each stamped with an official's name. Buyers and sellers in the market used the same stamped standard, so an argument over a coin could be settled on the spot. Why this matters: Fairness in small daily payments depended on everyone trusting the same measure.
why: Fairness in small daily payments depended on everyone trusting the same measure.
rights_status: open licence: Public domain (Met Open Access)

title: An old man and his young wife go to the arbitrators
hook: A Mughal painting of a married couple putting their quarrel before religious judges.
summary: This page illustrates a story from Saadi's Gulistan: an old man has married a young woman, the marriage is unhappy, and the case goes before men of religion to settle. Painted in India about 1610–15. Why this matters: It shows that a marriage dispute was something a wife could take outside the house to be heard.
why: It shows that a marriage dispute was something a wife could take outside the house to be heard.
rights_status: open licence: Public domain (Met Open Access)

title: A father and son argue before the judge of Sa'da
hook: A 13th-century painting of a family quarrel brought to the qadi in Yemen.
summary: In the Maqamat of al-Hariri, the trickster Abu Zayd and his son bring a dispute before the qadi of Sa'da. Readers loved these scenes: the judge listening, the crowd watching, everyone arguing their side. Why this matters: The court was a place where ordinary people, even family members, could make their case in public.
why: The court was a place where ordinary people, even family members, could make their case in public.

title: The judge in the black turban
hook: A 13th-century Maqamat page showing the qadi surrounded by the men who came to see him.
summary: This page from a Maqamat manuscript in the University of Manchester Library shows the qadi at the centre of a crowd. Judges heard debts, divorces, inheritance and neighbour disputes, often in a mosque or their own home. Why this matters: For most people the law was not a building; it was one person they could go to and ask to be heard.
why: For most people the law was not a building; it was one person they could go to and ask to be heard.

title: The deed that fed Jerusalem's poor
hook: Haseki Hürrem Sultan's endowment charter, written in Istanbul in 1556–57.
summary: A waqfiyya was a legal deed: it set aside property forever and said exactly who the income was for. Hürrem's endowments paid for, among other things, a public kitchen in Jerusalem that handed out soup and bread. Why this matters: One signed document kept food going to strangers long after the woman who signed it had died.
why: One signed document kept food going to strangers long after the woman who signed it had died.
creator: Unknown scribe

title: The soup kitchen the deed built
hook: The Haseki Sultan imaret in Jerusalem, funded by Hürrem's waqf.
summary: The kitchen founded under Hürrem's endowment became known for giving out food daily to the poor of the city. It is a living example of how a waqf deed turned into bread. Why this matters: It shows the law of endowments as something you could eat, not just read.
why: It shows the law of endowments as something you could eat, not just read.

title: A minister writes a deed for a whole neighbourhood
hook: The endowment deed of Rab'-e Rashidi in Tabriz.
summary: Rashid al-Din, a doctor and vizier in early-1300s Iran, endowed a quarter of Tabriz with a hospital, a school and a workshop for copying books. His deed set out salaries, food and rules for the people who lived and worked there. Why this matters: A waqf deed could plan a small town's welfare, from its doctors to its students' meals.
why: A waqf deed could plan a small town's welfare, from its doctors to its students' meals.
creator: Rashid al-Din

title: Free water and a school for orphans
hook: The sabil-kuttab of Sultan Mustafa III in Cairo.
summary: A sabil gave free drinking water to passers-by at a street window; the kuttab upstairs taught boys, often orphans, to read. Both were paid for by an endowment whose deed named the water-giver's and teacher's wages. Why this matters: Clean water and basic schooling were guaranteed by a legal promise, not by charity on a good day.
why: Clean water and basic schooling were guaranteed by a legal promise, not by charity on a good day.

title: A merchants' inn that paid for a fountain
hook: The wikala and sabil-kuttab of Sultan Qaitbay in Cairo.
summary: Traders slept, stored goods and did business in a wikala. Rent from these rooms was often written into a waqf so that it paid for a public fountain and a school in the same building. Why this matters: It ties trade and welfare together: merchants' rent became a city's water.
why: It ties trade and welfare together: merchants' rent became a city's water.
creator: Casual Builder (photo)

title: The kitchen of the Süleymaniye
hook: The imaret of the Süleymaniye complex, Istanbul.
summary: The Süleymaniye's founding deed listed who ate here: students, staff, travellers and the poor, with set rations of bread and soup. Today the old kitchen courtyard is a restaurant. Why this matters: An endowment deed decided who would be fed every day, and in what order.
why: An endowment deed decided who would be fed every day, and in what order.
creator: Dosseman (photo)

title: A marriage contract written for the bride
summary: Marriage contracts like this one named the mahr, the money or property promised to the bride, and were signed in front of witnesses. A woman kept her copy as proof of what she was owed. Why this matters: The contract was the bride's own legal document, enforceable in court.
why: The contract was the bride's own legal document, enforceable in court.
creator: Unknown calligrapher

title: The marriage contract of Malik Jahan Khanum
hook: An illuminated Qajar marriage contract dated 1833–34.
summary: Written in gold and ink for a granddaughter of Fath ʿAli Shah, this contract follows the same legal form as humbler ones: names, witnesses and the bride's mahr. Why this matters: Rich or poor, the bride's rights were set down in writing before the wedding.
why: Rich or poor, the bride's rights were set down in writing before the wedding.

title: A royal order kept as proof
hook: A Mughal decree with an illuminated heading, India, 1550.
summary: Firmans granted things to real people: land, a stipend, a tax exemption or permission to trade. Families and institutions kept them for generations and brought them out when their rights were questioned. Why this matters: A piece of paper was how an ordinary family could prove a promise made to them.
why: A piece of paper was how an ordinary family could prove a promise made to them.
rights_status: open licence: Public domain (Met Open Access)

title: A decree in the name of Dara Shikoh
hook: A Mughal order issued under Prince Dara Shikoh, 1649–50.
summary: Like other firmans, this order would have been read aloud, copied and filed, then held by the person it benefited. Princes' offices issued many of these for grants and appointments. Why this matters: Written orders made rights portable: you could carry them to the next official.
why: Written orders made rights portable: you could carry them to the next official.
rights_status: open licence: Public domain (Met Open Access)

title: A Qajar firman of 1831
hook: A royal decree of Fath ʿAli Shah.
summary: Qajar firmans confirmed grants, pensions and appointments. The seal and the formal heading showed any official that the order was genuine. Why this matters: The seal let a recipient defend their right without needing to know anyone powerful.
why: The seal let a recipient defend their right without needing to know anyone powerful.
rights_status: open licence: Public domain (Met Open Access)

title: A merchant's seal ring
hook: A seal ring with the name of Hajji Muhammad ibn Mahmud.
summary: Contracts, receipts and letters were sealed rather than signed. A man's seal ring carried his name and stood for his word; losing it was serious. Why this matters: A small ring made a person's promise checkable by anyone who saw the impression.
why: A small ring made a person's promise checkable by anyone who saw the impression.
rights_status: open licence: Public domain (Met Open Access)

title: A seal for signing agreements
hook: A seal ring with an inscription, Iran or Central Asia.
summary: Seal impressions appear on loan agreements, sale deeds and court records. Witnesses also sealed, which is how a deal between strangers could be trusted. Why this matters: Everyday contracts rested on these small marks of identity.
why: Everyday contracts rested on these small marks of identity.
rights_status: open licence: Public domain (Met Open Access)
